To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there are substantial international differences in the survival of people with cancer and that these differences are partly explained by differences in cancer registration.
variation in cancer registration practices can have a large impact on observed cancer survival differences between countries and that the impact of variation is larger for some cancers than others.

1) The ICBP-1 data showed that cancer survival was lower for all cancer sites and stages combined in the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia compared with Norway, Sweden, and Finland; 2) The ICBR-1 data showed lower cancer survival in the UK, Canada, and the USA compared with Norway and Sweden; and 3) The ICBRP data showed lower cancer-specific survival in the UK compared with the USA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of cancer registration practice on international comparisons of cancer survival.
the development of new mathematical and statistical methods for the analysis of large data sets, in particular those that arise in the context of the social and biomedical sciences.
the impact of variation in cancer registry practice in the International Cancer Benchmarking Project (ICBP) partner countries on observed survival differences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed international differences in cancer survival are largely attributable to differences in cancer registration practice, and not to differences in cancer survival.
the observed differences in cancer survival in the ICBP are likely to reflect differences in the quality of cancer registration practice.
the impact of variation in cancer registry practice is likely to be small and not a significant factor in explaining observed international differences in cancer survival between the ICBP countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that there is no evidence of a significant difference in the overall survival of cancer patients in the United Kingdom compared with other European countries and the United States.
the ICBP has provided an unprecedented level of information on cancer survival across the world, and has demonstrated the value of international comparisons to inform cancer policy.

the observed survival differences between countries are not solely due to differences in stage at diagnosis, but also due to differences in the quality of cancer care, including differences in treatment, supportive care and access to care.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the variation in cancer registration is not the primary reason behind the observed differences in survival between countries.
the observed survival difference between countries is not due solely to differences in the quality of care.
the ICBP is an important collaboration that has provided a unique opportunity for countries to compare their cancer survival data and to understand how these data are used in policy and practice.
